messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leo has not been able to pick up a tool without hesitation for six months. At thirty years old, carpentry isn't just his job; it's who he is. But the man who could once frame a house with confident precision now feels like a stranger in his own body. The accident, he calls it, though the word feels too small, too neat, for the memory that lives in his hands. He was sharing a thermos of sweet, milky coffee with his partner, Mark, when the table saw kicked back. The sound was one thing, but the image of Mark’s hand, instantly mangled, is what burned itself behind his eyes. In the chaos that followed, Leo was the one who grabbed shop rags and pressed down, trying to stop the bleeding. He remembers the unnatural warmth, the sickening give of the tissue, and the coppery taste of coffee and panic in his mouth as he waited for the ambulance. He has not been able to put the full horror of that moment into words since.

In the weeks that followed, Leo’s world began to shrink. The memory of the accident wasn't something he could recall; it was something that ambushed him. The sight of a customer with a bandaged finger at the lumber yard was enough to send him reeling, the scene replaying not as a thought but as a full-body experience. Suddenly, he would be back in the workshop, the smell of sawdust and blood in his nostrils, the phantom pressure of Mark’s ruined hand beneath his own palms. The sheer sensory force of these moments was terrifying, and in their wake, a cold certainty began to set in: he was permanently broken. This belief that he had been fundamentally changed for the worse became a lens through which he saw everything, making him scan his environment for danger, for any sign of injury that might confirm his fears.

This sense of being irreparably damaged now dictates his days. He has come to believe he can’t rely on himself, that his own mind is a minefield. This constant, anxious monitoring makes him exquisitely sensitive to new threats. A casual touch from his wife on his arm can feel electric, dangerous, immediately transporting him back to the workshop. That physical contact, meant as comfort, instead triggers a cascade of panic. In these moments, Leo’s only defense is to retreat. He will go to the kitchen and eat, mechanically and excessively, until the physical fullness crowds out the emotional terror. The distress of the memory is so absolute that he will do anything to escape it, often deliberately trying to make his mind go blank, to just float away from his body until the wave passes.

The strategies he uses to survive are now destroying his life, which only serves as further proof of his own brokenness. The overeating has led to a weight gain that makes his work clothes tight and his movements clumsy, reinforcing his feeling of being a failed, incompetent version of his former self. His attempts to dissociate leave his wife feeling shut out and him feeling even more disconnected from reality. These consequences feed directly into his darkest appraisals—that his life has been destroyed by the trauma and he is no longer the man he was. When a memory fragment intrudes, it feels less like a memory and more like a verdict, delivering irrefutable evidence of his own permanent damage. The more he believed he was broken, the more the memory seemed to surface, offering itself up as the primary exhibit in the case against himself. The vividness of the reliving makes the world outside feel saturated with danger, sensitizing him to things that were once benign.

Now, even the taste of the sugary coffee his wife makes him in the morning can plunge him back into that moment of horror. The trigger doesn't just bring back the memory; it brings with it the crushing weight of his belief that he is ruined beyond repair. He avoids talking about the accident, pushing away his wife’s attempts to connect, which only isolates him further. He came to therapy after a near-miss at work, where he’d frozen at the sound of a saw, lost in a memory, and nearly caused another accident. He is terrified of losing his job, of his wife finally giving up on him, but his deepest fear is that he is right—that the damage is done, and he will never be whole again.
